turns.doctor_question: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Yeah, so, what brings me in is... well, I'm a sales supervisor, and lately I just keep making these really dumb mistakes on our sales reports. Like, I'll be copying numbers over from the team dashboard—which, by the way, corporate just updated the software for that dashboard last month and it is an absolute nightmare. I really don't know why they always have to change things that are working just fine. My buddy Dave, he's one of my reps, he was saying the new interface actually gives him a headache, and I kind of agree, the colors are all washed out now. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Right, the reports. I'll copy the wrong numbers down, or I'll completely miss a line in a procedure I was supposed to check. And the crazy thing is, I swear I went over it. I'll look at it, think it's totally good to go, and then someone points out a glaring error. It's just getting really frustrating.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless mistakes on sales reports, such as copying wrong numbers or missing lines, despite believing they had checked their work.

turns.doctor_question: Have you struggled with this kind of difficulty focusing or making these types of mistakes throughout your life, or is this something that only started happening more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, it's definitely not a new thing. I was exactly like this as a kid too, actually. My mom still talks about all these teacher notes she used to get back in elementary school. She actually kept a bunch of them—which, I don't know why parents hold onto that kind of stuff, you know? She has this massive plastic storage bin that was just stuffed with old papers and macaroni art. I had to help her move a couple months ago into this smaller condo over in Westlake, and man, going through her garage was brutal. It was like ninety degrees out, and my back was killing me for a week after lifting those boxes. 

But anyway, yeah, she was going through that bin and pulling out these old notes saying how I always rushed through my work and constantly lost my homework. And that I talked out of turn all the time and couldn't stay seated without being reminded over and over. I had this one teacher, Mrs. Gable, who was super strict about the sitting still thing. She used to make us do this weird clapping routine to get our attention, and if you messed it up she'd make you stand by the chalkboard. I hated that chalkboard, the chalk dust always got all over my sleeves. 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, if it was recent. So yeah, I guess it's been happening pretty much my whole life.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient recalls childhood teacher notes stating they 'always rushed through my work,' indicating a tendency for careless mistakes.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions that they 'constantly lost my homework' during childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility during the interview by going on a long tangent about moving boxes and chalk dust, eventually forgetting the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient reports that as a child, they 'couldn't stay seated without being reminded over and over.'
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient notes that they 'talked out of turn all the time' in school, indicating interrupting or intruding on others.

turns.doctor_question: In your current day-to-day life as an adult, do you still feel a strong physical need to be moving or find it difficult to sit still for long periods, like in meetings or while relaxing?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, definitely. Sitting through a long meeting is... well, it honestly feels like my body is buzzing inside. I just can't stay put. I'm always shifting around in my chair, tapping my foot, or I'll just make up some excuse to go to the bathroom or grab water just so I can stand up. We actually have this new espresso machine in the breakroom—one of those fancy ones where you put the pods in, but it's not a Keurig, it's some Italian brand. It makes a ton of noise when it brews, which kind of annoys the HR lady whose office is right next door. She actually put a sticky note on it last week asking people not to use it during her Zoom calls. I mean, I get it, but also, we need our coffee, right? I tried switching to decaf for a while because my wife read this article saying caffeine makes you jittery, but honestly, it just gave me a headache. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, sitting still. Yeah, so I just have to get up and move, or I feel like I'm going to jump out of my skin.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by unrelated thoughts about an espresso machine and forgets the original topic of conversation.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly mentions shifting around in their chair and tapping their foot.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes making up excuses to leave their seat during long meetings just so they can stand up.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an internal feeling of restlessness, stating their body feels like it is 'buzzing inside' and they feel like they will 'jump out of my skin' if they don't move.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself blurting out answers before questions are completed or interrupting others while they are speaking?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I do that a lot, actually. Especially in meetings. I'll just jump right in before people even finish talking because I'm so sure I know where they're going with it. And then, half the time, I realize I completely answered the wrong point, or I just totally cut somebody off. It's really embarrassing. My manager actually pulled me aside after our quarterly review last week to talk about it. We were in the big conference room—the one with the huge glass windows that overlook the parking lot. Which, by the way, they've been repaving that lot for like three weeks now, and the smell of the tar is just awful. It seeps right through the vents. Plus, they blocked off half the spaces, so everyone is parking on the grass near the oak trees, and my car is getting covered in sap. I spent like twenty bucks at the car wash on Sunday trying to get it off, and the guy there told me I need to use rubbing alcohol, but I don't want to ruin the paint. It's a lease, you know? 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, blurting things out. Yeah, so I do that in meetings, and I end up cutting people off because I just can't hold the thought in.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by a chain of unrelated thoughts about a parking lot and car wash, causing them to forget the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly admits to jumping in and blurting out answers before people finish talking in meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient notes that they frequently cut people off during conversations because they cannot hold their thoughts in.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the restlessness and interrupting others, do you feel that your difficulty with staying focused and avoiding careless mistakes is the primary issue causing problems in your work and daily life?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I'd say it's definitely the main thing causing problems. Like, at work, it's gotten so bad that my manager actually put it in my formal review. Which, honestly, was a huge blow. I thought I was doing okay, you know? But seeing it on paper... they use this new software for the reviews now, Workday or something like that. It's supposed to make everything streamlined, but the interface is super clunky. I spent like two hours just trying to figure out how to submit my self-evaluation. The password requirements are insane, too. You need a capital letter, a number, a special character, and it can't be anything you've used in the last five years. I ended up writing it on a sticky note and putting it under my keyboard, which I know you're not supposed to do, but what else am I going to do? 

But yeah, at work it's in my review now. And at home, it's just... it adds to a lot of conflict. People feel like they can't count on me to follow through on things. Like I'll say I'm going to do something and then I just completely forget or get sidetracked.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient agrees with the doctor's question, confirming that their difficulty avoiding careless mistakes is a primary issue.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient confirms the doctor's premise that their difficulty staying focused is the main thing causing problems.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states that people feel they cannot count on them to 'follow through on things.'
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes that they often get 'sidetracked' instead of completing intended tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient admits that they 'completely forget' to do things they previously said they were going to do.

turns.doctor_question: When you look at your overall struggles, do you feel that your difficulty with staying focused and avoiding careless mistakes is just as significant as your struggle with feeling restless and interrupting others, or is one of those two areas clearly more problematic for you than the other?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, I couldn't really tell you if one is worse than the other. They just kind of feed into each other, you know? I don't really know how to weigh them. It's kind of like when I'm trying to balance the schedules for my sales team—I manage about twelve guys, mostly doing B2B industrial supply sales. Last week I was trying to organize this team-building thing for us at that new axe-throwing place downtown. Have you ever been to one of those? It's honestly a little crazy they just let anyone walk in off the street and throw axes. One of my guys, Dave, showed up in sandals, even though I'm pretty sure I told them to wear closed-toe shoes. Well, maybe I forgot to put it in the email. I do that a lot, just hit send before I actually finish typing all the important details. 

But anyway, the place was alright, except the food they catered was this really dry brisket. I don't get why people ruin good beef like that. You have to smoke it low and slow. I actually bought a Traeger smoker last summer, the one that uses the wood pellets? The cherry wood ones are the best, but they're getting so expensive at Home Depot. I went last weekend and a bag was like twenty-five bucks, which is just ridiculous inflation, man. I almost asked to speak to a manager, but I didn't have the time... 

Wait, sorry. What did you ask me? Oh, right, which problem is worse. Yeah, I don't know. I really don't have a clear answer for that, they both just mess me up about the same, I guess.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient agrees with the doctor's premise that his difficulty staying focused is a significant struggle that 'messes him up.'
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by getting sidetracked by his own unrelated thoughts about axe throwing and smokers, forgetting the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient agrees with the doctor's premise that his struggle with feeling restless is a significant problem.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, going on a long, unprompted tangent about his sales team, axe throwing, and a meat smoker.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient agrees with the doctor's premise that his struggle with interrupting others is a significant problem that 'messes him up.'
